In the primary text, there is no reference list, no individual author name printed (the text refers only to 'the Centre for Policy Studies (CPS)' and 'its author', never printing 'Latham'), no DOI, and no explicit citation year printed alongside the title (moreover, the blog post is dated September 2nd, 2013, states the report was published 'A fortnight ago', and notes its analysis period ended 31st May 2013, contradicting shipped's year '2012'). Blind coding accurately records the verbatim title printed in the text and leaves unprinted citation metadata blank per the codebook.

outcome.quote:
These numbers are all indicative, prior to any reliability testing, and, of course, they do not
   realistically provide evidence of the existence or absence of bias in the BBC any more than the
   CPS figures do. What they do represent is a fairly simple way to debunk the main conclusions
   drawn by the CPS from their own analysis and then spread by an overly­credulous press.
outcome.reason: In replicating the second part of the CPS report (coding BBC Online stories mentioning the ten think tanks for 'health warnings' and descriptions as 'independent'), the author obtained empirical proportions that mirrored the CPS findings ('the "health warning" proportions I found are relatively similar to those of the CPS'; 'This backs up the CPS conclusion that health warnings are more likely to be applied to right-wing think tanks, which are also less likely to be described as "independent"'; 'While the contextualisation data ("health warnings" and descriptions of independence) certainly mirror the CPS findings...'). However, the central thesis of the replication is that the CPS methodology and its omission of total mention counts (where right-wing think tanks actually accounted for 55% of mentions versus 45% for left/centre) mean those figures do not validly demonstrate ideological bias at the BBC, thereby debunking the main conclusions drawn by the CPS. Under the codebook, obtaining the original empirical effect while arguing as the main message that the original method/analysis does not validly support the substantive claim is coded as 'statistically successful but flawed' rather than 'failed'.

expected_before.outcome_quote: Regarding Racine and the Classical Age, it has become apparent that the stylistic patterns identified by Leo Spitzer, and which in the aggregate produce a dampening effect, again according to Spitzer, are even more frequent in Racine’s work than Spitzer showed. In addition, the analysis was able to show that these patterns are present in varying degrees in Racine’s work and in the work of his contemporaries, but without very strong (or statistically significant) differences, for the most part. The dampening effect, if understood as the aggregate use of individual stylistic patterns, is therefore clearly not an authorial signature style, but the mark of an entire literary genre during a certain period, at the very least.

Spitzer's original study was qualitative and non-digital, so exact computational reproduction of original numerical outputs was not checked. In the first phase re-analyzing the original 11 Racine plays via formal CQP queries in TXM on annotated texts, 24 of the roughly 50 stylistic patterns identified by Spitzer could be formally modeled (making the methodological transposition of the full 50-pattern catalog only partially feasible), and for those modeled patterns the analysis verified Spitzer's cited examples and showed that the dampening patterns are even more frequent in Racine's work than Spitzer showed (robust). original.quote:
This is a replication of Mayshar et al. (2022) (henceforth MMP).1 The article posits
that the state (defined as societal hierarchy such as tax-levying elites) originated from
cultivation of appropriable cereal grains, contrary to the conventional theory that the
state originated from increased land productivity following the adoption of agriculture.
The article uses multiple datasets to demonstrate a causal effect of cereal cultivation on
hierarchy (Claim 1) without finding a similar effect for land productivity (Claim 2), and
that societies based on roots or tubers display levels of hierarchy similar to nonfarming
societies (Claim 3).
original.location: Section 1 Introduction, p. 3, lines 128-135 (and References, p. 22, lines 2130-2131)
original.reason: The paper explicitly re-tests Mayshar, J., Moav, O., and Pascali, L. (2022), 'The origin of the state: Land productivity or appropriability?', Journal of Political Economy, 130(4):1091-1144 (lines 2130-2131). A Comment') as the original study. Blind coding correctly identified Mayshar et al. (2022) as target 0.

expected_before.outcome_quote: Although the stress induction was successful in both samples shown by increases of cortisol, heart rate, blood pressure and ratings of stress and arousal absent in the control condition, no state-dependent shift of RFA during stress induction was observed in either sample. The current study confirmed the relation between RFA at rest and cortisol, however the observed response pattern differed from the original study as RFA both pre-, and post- stress was significantly correlated to cortisol.

outcome.quote:
In conclusion, the current study could not confirm RFA as the state-dependent marker of emotional
processing as presented by Zhang et al. (2018). While RFA was again correlated to cortisol responses as
well as cardiovascular measures and subjective stress ratings indicating predictive power as a trait index,
the observed response pattern contradicted commonly accepted conceptualizations of RFA as
correlations were positive and not negative as predicted. Similarly, the previously reported state-
dependent changes in RFA could not be replicated in the current study. As such the current study
demonstrated the lack of replicability of studies supporting contemporary conceptualizations of RFA
even despite almost identical methodology.
outcome.reason: In the full-text conclusion, the author states an explicit overall failure-to-replicate verdict on Zhang et al. (2018), explaining that the state-dependent RFA shifts failed to replicate and that the trait RFA correlations with cortisol and stress ratings were in the opposite direction to the original findings. Under Rule 1, this overall verdict on the replication as a whole decides the outcome as failed despite the successful stress-induction manipulation check and an isolated heart-rate correlation.

In this second installment of
Data Replicada
, we report two attempts to replicate a study in a recently published
Journal of Consumer Research
(

original.reason: Parent independently inspected the entire DataColada post: its exact unique JournalOfConsumerResearch article title and specifically numbered study match this shipped original. Two new MTurk attempts retest that same finding; blank blind bibliographic fields do not establish an extra paper. Bind the existing original identity, with no unrequested outcome/type assignment.

outcome.quote: Let us first consider whether the original result was significant in the more highly powered replication attempts. In this case, the results are mixed. In the first replication attempt (with the typo), the three-way interaction among prime, group size, and preference for nonfiction was significant and in the same direction as in the original study: b = .162, SE = .070, p = .022. But in the second replication attempt (with no typo), that same interaction did not approach significance, though it was still in the same direction: b = .050, SE = .064, p = .432
outcome.reason: The shipped outcome ('successful') cherry-picked only the sentence reporting Replication 1 (which had a survey typo in the key dependent variable) while ignoring the immediately preceding sentence ('In this case, the results are mixed'), the failure to reach significance in Replication 2 (with the typo fixed, p = .432), and the concluding summary that the interaction 'may or may not be a real effect' and that its precise shape is inconsistent across studies and with the original theorizing. Under the codebook rules for aggregating multiple replication attempts of the same original study and following the authors' explicit characterization, the outcome is 'mixed'.

original.quote: In this sixth installment of Data Replicada, we report our attempt to replicate a recently published Journal of Consumer Research (JCR) article entitled, “The Impact of Resource Scarcity on Price-Quality Judgments” ( .html ). This one was full of surprises. The primary thesis of this article is straightforward: “Scarcity decreases consumers’ tendency to use price to judge product quality.” It reports six studies, three of which were conducted on MTurk. We chose to replicate Study 2A (N = 149) because it was the MTurk study with the strongest evidence, and because it also tested the effects of scarcity on two other measures: desire for abundance and categorization tendency (described below).
original.reason: The primary report explicitly identifies the replicated original study as the recently published Journal of Consumer Research article entitled 'The Impact of Resource Scarcity on Price-Quality Judgments' (specifically replicating Study 2A). Both the shipped row (input_row_index 2714) and blind coding (target_index 0) identify this exact article; the blind coding left author, year, and DOI fields blank only because the extracted blog post text replaced the hyperlink with '( .html )' and lacked a reference list. Other works mentioned in the post (Roux, Goldsmith, and Bonezzi 2015 for the borrowed scarcity writing prompt; Booth 1984 and Lynn 1991 in author feedback) are manipulation-source or background citations rather than replicated targets.

outcome.quote: On the one hand, we were successful at dramatically reducing attrition. On the other hand, we were unsuccessful at reducing differential attrition, as once again many more participants dropped out of the Scarcity condition than the Control condition. So then we gave up, and decided to call the whole thing “inconclusive.”
outcome.reason: Although the initial replication attempt produced statistically significant effects on price-quality correlation and categorization tendency (which the authors initially note 'looks like at least a partial success'), the authors demonstrate that severe differential attrition compromised random assignment and yielded a disproportionate share of 'Bad Responders' in the Scarcity condition, invalidating between-condition comparisons ('differential attrition means that we cannot validly compare Good Responders in the Control condition to Good Responders in the Scarcity condition... the jury is still out because a true test of this hypothesis would require conducting a study that eliminates the problem of differential attrition'). After a pre-registered follow-up study (N = 2,101) also failed to eliminate differential attrition, the authors state their overall verdict on the replication effort: 'So then we gave up, and decided to call the whole thing “inconclusive.”' Under the codebook, when the authors' own overall verdict is that a methodological defect (differential attrition compromising random assignment) prevents their attempt from providing a valid, meaningful test of the original hypothesis, the outcome is 'uninformative', not 'mixed'.

original.authors: Jahn, G.

corrected_value.title: Three turtles in danger: Spontaneous construction of causally relevant spatial situation models.

evidence.location: Introduction (q1), Hypotheses (q2), Design/Materials/Procedure (q6), and References (q23)
evidence.quote: To address these limitations, in 2022 I designed an online experiment closely following Jahn's (2004, Experiment 1) design and using Jahn's stimulus sentences translated into Bulgarian). Administration was individual and the order of sentences randomized. Unlike Bransford et al. (1972), I found no significant model type (same/different) by probe type (old/new) interaction effect on the recognition scores. Unlike Rinck et al. (2001), the main effect of model type for new sentences was not significant, although it was in the expected direction. Unlike Jahn (2004) there was no significant model type by scene type (predator/peaceful) interaction effect on recognition scores. Due to a bug in the experiment script, some sentence groups occurred more often than others. Now I aim to replicate Bransford et al.'s, Rinck et al.'s, and Jahn's results, with a new improved script and with a new set of participants.
evidence.reason: No prior adjudication or state files exist for this work. This prospective OSF registration closely follows the design and translated stimulus sentences of Jahn (2004, Experiment 1) in a new Bulgarian sample and explicitly retests Jahn's empirical findings: Confirmatory Hypothesis 2 tests the model-type main effect on new sentences (following Rinck et al., 2001 and Jahn, 2004) and Confirmatory Hypothesis 3 tests Jahn's (2004) specific model-type (same/different) by scene-type (predator/peaceful) interaction on new sentences. The reference list (q23) and Crossref metadata establish the original identity as Jahn, G. evidence.location: Abstract
evidence.quote: The present study systematically replicated the procedures of Drake et al. (2018) and employed the IRAP to assess general gender stereotypes among Japanese university students, who live in a society where gender inequality remains a pressing issue. In the IRAP procedure, participants responded to pairings of binary gender labels (female and male) and trait descriptors (feminine and masculine) by selecting “true” or “false” under instructions emphasizing rapid responding. Participants exhibited response patterns that were primarily pro-congruent with gender stereotypes, reflected in a consistent tendency to affirm matched gender label–trait pairings (i.e., female–feminine and male–masculine). No significant gender differences were found. Nevertheless, we discussed the possibility of stronger stereotype-consistent responses among male participants in pairings involving male labels, as implied by the current data. Correlational analyses were also conducted between the IRAP performances and scores on an explicit measure of egalitarian attitudes, although no clear correlations were found in the majority of analyses. Overall, the results generally replicated those of Drake et al. (2018), demonstrating stereotype-consistent responses in a Japanese sample.

to “Imagine that your country is preparing for the outbreak

proposed.” Subjects in the control condition are told: “If

B is adopted, there is one-third probability that 600 people
will be saved, and two-third probability that no people will
be saved.” Subjects in the treatment group (the “mortality
frame”) are told: “If Program A is adopted, 400 people will
die. If Program B is adopted there is one-third probability
that nobody will die, and two-third probability that 600 people will die.”

blind_target.authors: Bertenthal, B., & Fisher, K.
blind_target.title: Development of self-recognition in the infant.
blind_target.evidence_quote: Numerous developmental studies of predominantly urban Western middle-class children suggest that children reach this milestone by 18 to 24 months of age. By 18 months, approximately 50% pass and by 24 months a significant majority of children (more than 70%) are reported to self- refer by touching or removing a mark from their own body (face or other body region) while exploring their mirror image (Amsterdam, 1972; Asendorpf, Warkentin, & Baudonnière, 1996; Bard, Todd, Bernier, Love, & Leavens, 2006; Bertenthal & Fisher, 1978; Lewis & Brooks-Gunn, 1979; Lewis & Ramsay, 2004; Nielsen, Dissanayake, & Kashima, 2003; Schulman & Kaplowitz, 1976). Here we report cross-cultural observations on the emergence of mirror self-recognition (MSR), using a simplified mark test, raising questions regarding the meaning and universal validity of this test as an ontogenetic benchmark of self-concept. The basic rationale behind the mark test is that when a child is marked surreptitiously and attempts to touch the mark on the body, as opposed to doing nothing or trying to reach for it on the mirror surface, it indicates that the specular image stands for the child’s own body. Self-oriented gestures are taken as the behavioral index of self-recognition, indicating that the embodied self is the referent of what is seen in the mirror (Rochat, 2003). In a different account, Nielsen, Suddendorf, and Slaughter (2006) claim that the mark test is passed by individuals who have a rapidly updatable image of themselves that they recognize in the mirror. Regardless of the rela- tive validity of these accounts, the general consensus is that passing the mark test indicates that children recognize their image and that those who fail the test do not. From a comparative perspective, chimpanzees, orangutans, dolphins, and Asian elephants are among the few nonhuman species reported to pass the mark test (Gallup, 1982; Plotnik & de Waal, 2006; Povinelli, 1995; Reiss & Marino, 1998). Nonhuman individuals passing the test typically have extensive prior experience with reflective surfaces. In contrast, research with humans suggests that children’s relative familiarity with mirrors, which greatly varies across contexts, does not correlate with the age at which the mark test is passed (Priel & deSchonen, 1986). Priel and deShonen (1986) tested Bedouin nomadic children with no previous mirror experience and compared them to same-age Israeli children familiar with mirrors. They found no significant difference in the developmental onset of MSR between mirror familiar and unfa- miliar children. However, more recent cross-cultural studies point to significant cultural variations in the onset of MSR. Keller and collaborators compared 18- to 20-month-olds from urban Greece, Costa Rica, Germany, as well as from a rural community in Cameroon, and they report a greater proportion of German, Greek, and Costa Rican children passing the test (more than 50%), compared to Cameroonian children (less than 4%) (Keller, Kartner, Borke, Yovsi, & Kleis, 2005; Keller et al., 2004). These authors correlate such variations to variations in par- enting strategies that exist across these cultures, fostering more or less autonomy in the young child. If such variability is validated with other cultures, testing children older than 18 to 20 months would allow us to determine whether this variability pertains only to a developmental delay, pos- sibly resulting from variations in parenting styles (see Keller et al., 2005; Keller et al., 2004) or whether such differences persist throughout development. If the latter is the case, this would sug- gest that there may be culture-specific responses to the passing of the mirror mark test (i.e., greater occurrence of potential false negatives). To probe this alternative explanation, we per- formed two experiments testing (a) whether cross-cultural variability in the passing of the mirror mark test could be verified across more cultures and (b) whether such variability would persist beyond the age at which children typically are reported to pass the mirror mark test. In two experiments, we tested children 18 to 72 months old living in seven distinct cultural groups. Because of the exploratory nature of this work, aside from probing these questions, no specific hypotheses were made.
blind_target.outcome_quote: The second experiment demonstrates that a significant amount of variability exists across cultural contexts in children’s behavioral response to this version of the MSR test that measures spontaneous self-recognition (see also Lewis & Ramsey, 2004). Consistent with past research, 77% to 88% of Western children (Canada and United States) pass this version of the MSR test by spontaneously displaying self-oriented behaviors. In contrast, only half of the children from Saint Lucia, Grenada, or Peru and none of the Fijian children of the same age showed any sign of such behaviors.

Self-oriented gestures are taken as the behavioral index of self-recognition, indicating that the embodied self is the referent of what is seen in the mirror (Rochat, 2003). In a different account, Nielsen, Suddendorf, and Slaughter (2006) claim that the mark test is passed by individuals who have a rapidly updatable image of themselves that they recognize in the mirror. Regardless of the rela- tive validity of these accounts, the general consensus is that passing the mark test indicates that children recognize their image and that those who fail the test do not. From a comparative perspective, chimpanzees, orangutans, dolphins, and Asian elephants are among the few nonhuman species reported to pass the mark test (Gallup, 1982; Plotnik & de Waal, 2006; Povinelli, 1995; Reiss & Marino, 1998). Nonhuman individuals passing the test typically have extensive prior experience with reflective surfaces. In contrast, research with humans suggests that children’s relative familiarity with mirrors, which greatly varies across contexts, does not correlate with the age at which the mark test is passed (Priel & deSchonen, 1986). Priel and deShonen (1986) tested Bedouin nomadic children with no previous mirror experience and compared them to same-age Israeli children familiar with mirrors. They found no significant difference in the developmental onset of MSR between mirror familiar and unfa- miliar children. However, more recent cross-cultural studies point to significant cultural variations in the onset of MSR. Keller and collaborators compared 18- to 20-month-olds from urban Greece, Costa Rica, Germany, as well as from a rural community in Cameroon, and they report a greater proportion of German, Greek, and Costa Rican children passing the test (more than 50%), compared to Cameroonian children (less than 4%) (Keller, Kartner, Borke, Yovsi, & Kleis, 2005; Keller et al., 2004). These authors correlate such variations to variations in par- enting strategies that exist across these cultures, fostering more or less autonomy in the young child. If such variability is validated with other cultures, testing children older than 18 to 20 months would allow us to determine whether this variability pertains only to a developmental delay, pos- sibly resulting from variations in parenting styles (see Keller et al., 2005; Keller et al., 2004) or whether such differences persist throughout development. If the latter is the case, this would sug- gest that there may be culture-specific responses to the passing of the mirror mark test (i.e., greater occurrence of potential false negatives). To probe this alternative explanation, we per- formed two experiments testing (a) whether cross-cultural variability in the passing of the mirror mark test could be verified across more cultures and (b) whether such variability would persist beyond the age at which children typically are reported to pass the mirror mark test. In two experiments, we tested children 18 to 72 months old living in seven distinct cultural groups. Because of the exploratory nature of this work, aside from probing these questions, no specific hypotheses were made.
blind_target.outcome_quote: The second experiment demonstrates that a significant amount of variability exists across cultural contexts in children’s behavioral response to this version of the MSR test that measures spontaneous self-recognition (see also Lewis & Ramsey, 2004). Consistent with past research, 77% to 88% of Western children (Canada and United States) pass this version of the MSR test by spontaneously displaying self-oriented behaviors. In contrast, only half of the children from Saint Lucia, Grenada, or Peru and none of the Fijian children of the same age showed any sign of such behaviors.

original.authors: McNiel, J. M., & Fleeson, W.

corrected_value.title: The causal effects of extraversion on positive affect and neuroticism on negative affect: Manipulating state extraversion and state neuroticism in an experimental approach
corrected_value.title_o: The causal effects of extraversion on positive affect and neuroticism on negative affect: Manipulating state extraversion and state neuroticism in an experimental approach
corrected_value.evidence_quote: Although possible, two studies have assessed negative affect under similar circumstances and have failed to find the state by trait interaction that would suggest a mood cost for acting counterdispositionally (McNiel & Fleeson, 2006; McNiel et al., 2010). On the other hand, one of these samples was small (n⫽45) and both employed a within-subject design that could promote demand or carryover effects. In fact, the studies did find significant order effects and some inconsistent trait and acting condition effects on negative affect. So although there was not a significant interaction suggesting an affective cost, the full mood consequences of acting more or less extraverted require some clarification, particularly with regard to negative affect. Therefore, our studies include between-subjects manipulations, larger sample sizes, and measures of both positive and negative affect to better assess any possible distress that might accompany counterdispositional behavior.
corrected_value.outcome_quote: Results replicated and extended past findings suggesting that acting extraverted produces hedonic benefits regardless of disposition. Positive affect increased and negative affect did not, even for participants acting out of character.

blind_target.title: Cultural preferences for formal versus intuitive reasoning
blind_target.evidence_quote:
20. Preferences for formal versus intuitive reasoning (Norenzayan, Smith, Kim, & Nisbett, 2002, Study 2). The way people living in the West think may be more rule based than the way people living in East Asia think. Fiftytwo European Americans (27 men, 25 women), 52 Asian Americans (28 men, 24 women), and 53 East Asians (27 men, 26 women) were randomly assigned to either a classification-judgment condition (decide "which group the target object belongs to"; two thirds of the sample) or a similarity-judgment condition (decide "which group the target object is most similar to"; one third of the sample).
All participants categorized targets into two alternative groups. Each stimulus set consisted of two targets and two groups of four exemplars each. Each of the two target stimuli was presented separately with the two groups. All the exemplars in each group had a particular feature in common with each other and with one of the targets but shared a family resemblance, and no single common feature, with the other target, in a counterbalanced design (see Fig. 1). When asked "which group the target object belongs to," European American and East Asian participants preferred to classify on the basis of a rule (M = 69% of responses for European Americans; M = 70% of responses for East Asians) rather than family resemblance, F(1, 100) = 44.40, p < .001, r = .55. When asked "which group the target object is more similar to," European Americans gave many more responses based on the unidimensional rule (M = 69%) than on family resemblance (M = 31%), t(17) = 3.68, p = .002, d = 1.65, 95% CI = [0.59, 2.67]. In contrast, East Asians gave fewer rule-based responses (M = 41%) than family-resemblance-based responses (M = 59%), t(17) = -2.09, p = .05, d = -0.93, 95% CI = [-1.85, 0.01]. The responses of Asian Americans were intermediate, with participants indicating no preference for the unidimensional rule (M = 46%) over family resemblance (M = 54%), t < 1.
Replication. For the replication, we preregistered a plan to compare the percentage of rule-based responses between the belong-to and similar-to conditions. In the original study, European Americans showed no difference between these conditions (d = 0.00, 95% CI = [-0.15, 0.15]), but East Asians were more likely to give rulebased responses in the belong-to condition than in the similar-to condition (d = 0.67, 95% CI = [0.52, 0.81). Note that we planned a comparison between the experimental conditions, whereas Norenzayan et al. (2002) focused their analysis and theoretical interest on comparisons between cultural groups within each experimental condition.
We computed the percentage of rule-based responses for each participant and then tested whether the mean percentages for the two experimental conditions were equal, using a t test for independent samples. In the aggregate replication sample (N = 7,396), participants who were asked "which group the target object belongs to" were more likely to classify on the basis of a rule (M = 64%, SD = 25%) than on the basis of family resemblance (M = 36%, SD = 25%), and participants who were asked "which group the target object is more similar to" were more likely to classify on the basis of family resemblance (M = 56%, SD = 21%) than on the basis of a rule (M = 44%, SD = 21%). The likelihood of using a rule was higher in the belong-to condition compared with the similar-to condition, t(7227.59) = 37.05, p = 3.04e -275 , d = 0.86, 95% CI = [0.81, 0.91]. This pattern was in the same direction as the original aggregate result, and the effect size was somewhat larger: People were more likely to categorize on the basis of a rule when they considered what group the target belonged to and more likely to categorize on the basis of family resemblance when they considered what group the target was similar to. 5 Follow-up analyses. We identified a priori that this effect and the one reported by Tversky and Gati (1978) both involved similarity judgments and thus that the order of these study materials in Slate 2 might be particularly relevant. We tested whether Norenzayan et al.'s (2002) effect was moderated by whether its materials came before or after Tversky and Gati's and observed very weak moderation by task order, t(7392) = 2.34, p = .02, d = 0.05, 95% CI = [0.01, 0.10].

The qualification about the original theoretical commitment does not erase that stated contrast. Neither comparison is an overall replication verdict.

evidence.location: Abstract, line 37 (and Background, lines 72-87; Method and Results, lines 96-185; Discussion, lines 188-198; References, lines 205-209)
evidence.quote: To shed light on the different findings, we carry out a replication using a unique dataset from the UK, which tracks individual purchases of food and drinks for out of home consumption over a period of three years. Similar to Gullo et al. (2019), we found variety-seeking increases from the morning to the afternoon. Additionally, we found a post-lunch dip. Our results as such lend further support to the matching mechanism between variety-seeking and diurnal level proposed by Gullo et al. (2019) rather than the compensating mechanism suggested by Roehm and Roehm (2004).
evidence.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. Luna triage mistakenly conflated target_index 1 (Gullo et al., 2019) with the sibling target Roehm and Roehm (2004) (shipped row '1493'). In fact, Trinh (2025) explicitly frames and conducts the study as an empirical replication designed to adjudicate the conflicting time-of-day variety-seeking findings of both Roehm and Roehm (2004) and Gullo, Berger, Etkin, and Bollinger (2019, Journal of Consumer Research 46(1):20-35, DOI 10.1093/jcr/ucy061). Specifically, Trinh (2025) retests Gullo et al.'s (2019) full-day (6 am to 11 pm) continuous non-linear diurnal pattern using polynomial regressions across three variety-seeking measures (brand count, Entropy, and reversed HHI; Figs. 1-3, Table 1), confirming Gullo et al.'s finding that variety-seeking increases from morning to early afternoon (6 am to 1 pm) and supporting Gullo et al.'s diurnal matching mechanism. The sole shipped row (input_row_index '1493', Roehm & Roehm, 2004, Marketing Letters 15:213-221, DOI 10.1007/s11002-005-0457-y) is a separate 2004 paper by different authors in a different journal reporting the opposite effect, so report equivalence does not apply and Gullo et al. (2019) is a genuinely absent replication target.

evidence.quote:
However, we did hypothesise an interaction, such that
an n+2 preview effect would be observed in the idioms, but not the phrases. We made this
hypothesis on the basis that idioms may have multi-word unit representational status, such
that the first character of the idiom may licence the processing of the entire unit (idiom), thus
leading to the early extraction of information from word n+2. In contrast the first character of
a phrase should not licence the processing of a larger lexical unit (the phrase) and therefore
the early extraction of information from word n+2. In this way the second constituent of an
idiom would be processed in the parafovea despite the processing difficulty of the first
constituent, in a similar manner to the second constituent of a spaced compound in Cutter et
al.’s (2014) study. If this did occur, it would be strong evidence for the idioms being
parafoveally processed as a multi-word unit.

evidence.reason: Current Experiment2 prospectively tests Cutter2014specific multi-word-unit parafoveal preview finding: low-frequency first constituents should permit terminal preview when the unit is lexicalized. This is an actual conceptual retest, despite the authors reserving an overall replication label for the Yangbenchmark in Experiment1. The empirical claim is not mere use of a reading task or interactive-activation theory. Temperament and Character Dimensions (Cloninger, 1987) and the Big Five personality index.

conscientiousness, r(128) = .46, p < .001, d = 1.04, 95% CI = [.64, 1.43].

replicate the relation between persistence and conscientiousness, we used the unsolvable 

anagram task, which has been used as a measure of persistence (e.g., Aspinwall & Richter, 1999; 

Sommer & Baumeister, 2002).  In this task, participants are presented with a number of 

anagrams to unscramble.  Some anagrams are solvable, others are not.  Participants choose to 

stop working on the task whenever they would like.  Persistence is the amount of time spent on 

the task before moving on to the next task.   

Unlike the others, this is not a direct replication.

evidence.quote:
researchers such as Howarth (1998b) and Ackerman and Chen (2013) that lexical
collocations are more difficult than grammatical collocations to master and the claim
that grammatical collocations are more easily internalised because they are more
predictable (Ackerman & Chen, 2013). My findings also partially corroborate Gitsaki’s

evidence.reason: Toomer (2019; shipped row 2422 year_r=2021; duplicate row 2456 removed) Experiment 2 (Ch. 4) conceptually re-tests Gitsaki’s (1999) specific empirical finding that previously encountered V+N collocations yield lower gap-fill scores than prep+N collocations. Section 2.1.1 (p. 9) attributes to Gitsaki (1999) an empirical study of 275 Greek junior high school learners tested on textbook collocations where gap-fill production was less accurate for V+N than prep+N. Experiment 2 tests 78 Chinese learners on 43 analysed (21 V+N, 22 prep+N) collocations repeated six times under bolded vs. unbolded reading; gap-fill accuracy was lower for V+N than prep+N when bolded (17.91% vs. 30.91%, z=-4.78, p<.001, Tables 15 & 19; p. 130 prose reverses this direction) but not unbolded (15.80% vs. 17.96%, z=-0.24, p=.99; interaction z=3.08, p=.002, Table 17). Section 5.3.6 (p. 163) explicitly states that Experiment 2 partially corroborates Gitsaki’s gap-fill ordering, distinct from general learnability claims (Howarth, 1998b; Ackerman & Chen, 2013), and notes no prior study compared enhanced and unenhanced L2 lexical and grammatical collocation learning. Shipped row 2422 represents only Sonbul & Schmitt (2013) (adj+N/N+N medical collocations), so Gitsaki (1999) is genuinely absent. Catalog and Google Books records (0236, ISBN 1573093890) verify the 1999 primary empirical book and its 275-learner blank-filling study, while its internal numeric rankings (and equivalence to the restricted 1996 thesis, not substituted here) are not independently read from the book body and rest on Toomer’s explicit attribution.

evidence.location: Discussion - Summary of Findings and Institutional Characteristics and Emerging Adulthood (lines 781-815); Results - Demographic Controls (lines 590-618, Table 4); References (lines 1121-1125)
evidence.quote:
Additionally, women rated Normative Compliance and Relational Maturity as more

important indicators of adulthood, and they reported higher achievement of Normative

Compliance. This result supports prior findings of higher ratings of importance for Normative

Compliance items for women among both American and Chinese participants, though no other

sex differences were reported (Badger et al., 2006). Other research also documented women

rating Normative Compliance as more important than men did, though they also found women

rated other constructs as important for this transition (Nelson et al., 2007). The lack of difference

in achievement in our sample is a curious finding that should be further considered, but the

pattern of perceived importance seems consistent with prior literature.

Institutional Characteristics and Emerging Adulthood

       Although replication of these age and gender effects are important, it was the replication

of associations with institutional selectivity and liberal arts status that represented our primary

questions. Specifically, we replicated Fosse and Toyokawa (2016) who first examined these

variables.
evidence.reason: Using independent multi-site survey data from EAMMi2 (N = 1,572 students across 23 institutions), the authors empirically tested age and gender fixed effects across all four Markers of Adulthood importance and achievement subscales in Results ('Demographic Controls', lines 590-618, Table 4) and explicitly state in the Discussion that they 'replicated previously observed age and gender differences in markers of adulthood (Badger et al., 2006, Nelson et al., 2007)' (lines 781-782) and refer to the 'replication of these age and gender effects' (line 809). They directly compare their gender results (women rating Normative Compliance and Relational Maturity as more important and reporting higher Normative Compliance achievement) to Badger, S., Nelson, L. J., & Barry, C. M. (2006), 'Perceptions of the transition to adulthood among Chinese and American emerging adults', International Journal of Behavioral Development, 30(1), 84-93, doi:10.1177/0165025406062128, which reported higher female importance ratings for Normative Compliance among Chinese and American emerging adults with no other sex differences. Fosse and Toyokawa (2016) is not an intermediary replication chain for these effects because it treated biological sex and age only as covariates when testing institutional selectivity and liberal arts status (lines 186-190, 809-817). The only shipped row (input_row_index 2425, originally citing the psychometric manuscript Fosse, Grahe, & Reifman, 2016, and source-adjudicated to target_index 0, Fosse & Toyokawa, 2016) and sibling target_index 2 (Nelson et al., 2007, a separate Journal of Family Psychology study of emerging adults and their parents) are distinct works, so report equivalence does not apply. evidence.quote: Previously, Eimer et al. (2009) had observed an enhanced N2 component in response to color-cues that did not match the target cues. Thus, the most straightforward prediction is that an enhanced N2 occurs for neutral and nogo cues alike because both do not match the go-color.

blind_target.title: The roles of feature-specific task set and bottom-up salience in attentional capture: an ERP study.
blind_target.evidence_quote: Previously, Eimer et al. (2009) had observed an enhanced N2 component in response to color-cues that did not match the target cues. Thus, the most straightforward prediction is that an enhanced N2 occurs for neutral and nogo cues alike because both do not match the go-color.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Of importance, Eimer et al. (2009) showed that the negativity at anterior electrodes was larger with non-matching than matching cues, suggesting that inhibition occurred when cues did not match the top–down set. Similarly, we observed a larger negativity for non-matching nogo cues. However, the negativity was the same for neutral cues, which suggests that the N2 does not reflect inhibition of nogo-stimuli, but rather activation of response-relevant stimuli (see Bruin et al., 2001 ).
